text: Most AI use cases start with a very simple question. What can AI help me do? But with agents, a more important question is, what work is worth handing over for AI to carry forward across multiple steps? A technically possible agent can still be a very poor use case. Your first agentic workflow should matter enough to justify the effort, but be contained enough that you can understand, test and also supervise it. One common mistake that we see is that people start with a role, like I want a sales agent or I want an AI project manager. And that is usually too broad. Instead, we want to start with a workflow. We want one specific piece of work with a clear starting point, a defined result and clear boundaries. So now instead of manage my customer accounts, you may choose something like after a customer meeting, review the notes, identify the commitments, check your relevant account information, prepare to follow up and flag anything that needs human judgment. Now you've built something that you can actually assess. Now even with agents, GEDRT is the most useful starting point for finding work that's worth giving to AI so that you can shift more of your time and attention toward your North Star and the work where you create the most impact. This means looking for work that again is general, error friendly, digital, repetitive and toil. But a gantic delegation adds another design challenge. Because if AI is going to carry a workflow forward across multiple steps, there's three can you clearly define what the agent is responsible for, where that responsibility ends and when a person needs to step in. The second is, is it testable? Can you tell whether the agent completed the work correctly, including the important steps and decisions along the way? And the third is, is it actually technically feasible? Can the platform that you are using actually access the right information, connect with the right tools and perform the actions that the workflow requires? Together that gives you the agentic fit check. You start with a strong GEDRT workflow and then you check that it is bounded, testable and feasible to implement. Now one thing we want to do is choosing the smallest impactful workflow and this matters because broad workflows hide problems. If you create an agent to quote unquote manage customer relationships, you're going to leave too many decisions, too many actions and too many boundaries undefined. But a specific post meeting follow up workflow gives you something that you can observe, test and improve. So when you're choosing your first agentic use case, don't look for the biggest process that you could automate. Look for the smallest meaningful workflow that passes GEDRT and is bounded, testable and feasible. And that is really the kind of work worth delegating to an agent.
